title: Q (worked examples): de Broglie Wavelength & Uncertainty Principle
topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: **Q1. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s.** Using λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and v = 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s: λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.6 × 10⁶) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.006 × 10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

**Q2. Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball (mass ≈ 0.15 kg) not observable?** Using λ = h/(mv), for even a small ball travelling at 30 m/s the wavelength is λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 30) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻³⁴ m — far smaller than the size of a nucleus and completely unobservable; the wavelength is negligible for macroscopic objects (λ ∝ 1/m).

**Q3. If the uncertainty in the position of an electron is 10⁻¹⁰ m, what is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity?** Using Δx · Δv ≥ h/(4πm): Δv = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (4 × 3.14 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 1.143 × 10⁻³⁹ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s.

**Q4. Explain why Bohr's definite orbits contradict the uncertainty principle.** A definite orbit requires both position and momentum to be exactly known at every instant, but Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π forbids simultaneous exact knowledge — so the electron cannot follow a sharply defined circular path.
